legal.headline: No tort law, only tort rulings—India’s liability framework grew case by case through courts & tribunals
legal.hook: No tort law, only tort rulings—India’s liability framework grew case by case through courts & tribunals ThePrint
legal.summary: The article examines India's approach to tort law and liability, highlighting that India lacks a codified, comprehensive tort statute comparable to statutory frameworks in contract or criminal law. Instead, India's liability framework has developed organically through case-by-case judicial rulings and tribunal decisions across the Supreme Court, High Courts, and specialized tribunals. The piece appears to trace how courts and tribunals have incrementally shaped tort principles—covering negligence, breach of duty, damages, and remedies—rather than through legislative codification. The article discusses how this common law-influenced, jurisprudential approach has created the practical liability rules that govern tort disputes in India. It underscores that Indian tort liability remains judge-made law, with each significant judgment contributing layers to an evolving framework that practitioners must navigate through case law rather than statutory text.
legal.contextNote: India's tort law operates through common law principles embedded in case precedent rather than a unified tort code (unlike, say, contract law under the Indian Contract Act, 1872). Key cases from Rylands v. Fletcher interpretations, negligence standards post-Donoghue v. Stevenson adoption, and more recent Supreme Court judgments on tortious liability, vicarious liability, and damages constitute the operative framework. For corporate counsel at entities like Reliance or fintech startups, this matters because: (1) product liability, environmental damage, and workplace injury claims rely on judicially-articulated standards with evolving scope; (2) NCLT and specialized tribunals increasingly apply tort principles to commercial disputes; (3) regulatory bodies (SEBI, CCI, ED) sometimes layer tortious concepts onto administrative actions. A lawyer should monitor recent Supreme Court and High Court judgments that expand or narrow tort liability, especially in sectors affecting large corporates (product safety, pollution, data harm under DPDP Act). This fragmented framework poses advisory risk—clients need precedent-based counsel, not statutory certainty.
